**Paper Summary.**
The paper is motivated to facilitate biodiversity monitoring particularly for detecting/recognizing unknown species, which can be formulated as an open-set recognition (OSR) problem. To foster OSR research in this more applicable context, the paper curates the new dataset called Open-Insect, sampling moth images based on the AMI dataset [37] with region tags (North America, Western Europe, and Central America). It uses the AMI-GBIF dataset as in-distribution data, and compiles 28,388 moth species as out-of-distribution and auxiliary data. It studies 38 OSR algorithms and analyzes their results, leading to several technical insights.

**Review Summary.**
Three reviewers evaluated this paper. After rebuttal and author-reviewer discussion, all the three reviewers raised the rating to Accept. The reviewers recognize certain merits in the paper: the dataset itself, the motivation, writing quality, and extensive experiments. Reviewers requested for new results and discussions, e.g., using modern metrics and using foundation models, and comparing Open-Insect and the existing BIOSCAN datasets. These results and discussions are important and the authors provided them in the rebuttal. As such, AC encourages the authors to incorporate them in the final version. Yet, there are a couple of remaining concerns summarized below-

 - The authors are expected to provide curves w.r.t OSCR metric as this metric offers opportunities for more in-depth analysis, e.g., the operating points can tell how to deploy developed models in real biodiversity monitoring scenarios.

 - The authors are expected to finalize citations and the formats. Some cited arxiv papers have been officially published so it is good to cite in their official version.

**Decision.**
Based on the above, the AC recommends accepting this paper.

===== FINAL UPDATE FROM DB Track PCs ====

The final decision for this paper has been taken by the program chairs after consultation with the SACs. All Senior Area Chairs have ranked papers according to the feedback from the AC during the review process. We decided to leave the original meta-review to reflect the opinion of the AC in light of the initial discussions with reviewers and SAC.

Thank you for the suggestion on using more modern metrics. We will include OOSA, OpenAUC, and AUOSRC in the final version. 

Also, thank you for clarifying the difference between OOSA and OSA. Our current results were computed using the test set, which corresponds to OSA. We will recompute the metric using the auxiliary validation set to report both OSA and OOSA in the final version. The tables below present the OSR performance of MSP evaluated with various metrics.

Thank you for your rebuttal. Indeed, there is typically a strong correlation between metrics, but there are some cases where they do not correlate well, so it is always advisable to use the more modern metrics.

For the final version, it would be required to report how **Operational** Open-Set Accuracy (OOSA) was computed. OOSA requires an external "surrogate" set to determine the threshold. If such a surrogate dataset does not exist, and the authors have used the test set to compute the threshold, the metric is called Open-Set Accuracy (OSA).

Similarly, OSCR refers to the curve. What the authors are likely reporting here is the **Area Under** the OSCR curve, i.e., AUOSCR.

# Evaluation metrics
Thank you for your valuable feedback regarding the evaluation metrics. We have updated our experiments to include OSCR, OpenAUC, and OOSA. 

## Results
Due to character limitations, we cannot show results for all methods across all three regions. Instead, we provide a summary by presenting the rank of each method based on different evaluation metrics and the correlation between AUROC and the other three metrics. 

### Correlation
We find that AUROC has a positive correlation with all of the other metrics. 

|         |   Correlation |
|:--------|--------:|
| OSCR    |    0.73 |
| OpenAUC |    0.73 |
| OOSA    |    0.84 |

### Ranking Methods Across Metrics
For each method, we first computed the mean of each metric (AUROC, OSCR, OpenAUC, and OOSA) across all regions (NE-America, W-Europe, and C-America) and OOD splits (local, non-local, and non-moth). Based on the mean, we assigned a rank to each method per metric. Finally, we calculated the mean and standard deviation of these ranks across the four metrics to summarize each method’s overall performance and the consistency across different metrics within the three categories: 1) post-hoc, 2) training regularization, and 3) training with extra data.


The columns named "AUROC", "OSCR", "OpenAUC", and "OOSA" show the mean rank of each method when evaluated using the corresponding metric. These tables show that the four metrics are relatively consistent on evaluating the OSR performance of different methods, as indicated by the small standard deviations.

# Explainability
Thank you for this excellent question. We recognize that discussions on the explainability of the methods can be very helpful when encouraging domain experts to adopt ML-based tools for species discovery. 

We would like to clarify that both the ID and OOD data were sourced from a variety of origins, including museums, research institutions, and community science platforms, all accessed through GBIF. The benchmark was intentionally designed to not have ID data from some specific labs or camera traps and OOD data from others.

To additionally respond to your question, we conducted an experiment to empirically verify that **background features are not enough to achieve good OSR performance on Open-Insect.** Specifically, we masked the insect or the background in a subset of images and ran our C-America classifier on this subset and evaluated the accuracy of the model on the ID dataset and the OSR performance of maximum softmax score (MPS), a well-performing post-hoc method. (Further details below.)

Using the original images gives the highest ID accuracy (ACC) and the best OSR performance (AUROC). When the insect was masked, the model was forced to rely solely on the background and the insect's silhouette. ACC dropped to just 1.63%, and AUROC decreased to 46.57, close to 50% (the performance of a random classifier). When the background is masked, the model still achieved performance comparable to that on the original images, though ACC and AUROC decreased by 4% and 6.87%, respectively.


| Test Data              | AUROC (MSP)|  ACC  | 
|---------------------|--------|-------|
| Original  image          | 80.01  | 71.01 | 
| Moth masked         | 46.57  |  1.63 | 
| Background masked   | 76.01  | 64.14 | 




In the above experiment, we constructed the dataset as follows. We first used Grounding DINO to detect and generate a bounding box around the insect in each image, then used it as an input prompt to SAM, which segmented the insect. Finally, we replaced the segmented region with the average value of the surrounding pixels. We applied this pipeline to a subset of Open-Insect C-America. Since both object detection and segmentation were done by models, errors can occur. Hence, we manually verified a (randomized) subset of the processed images and discarded the rest, ultimately obtaining 859 valid ID and 1433 valid local OOD images for our experiments. 


We believe the slight drop of performance when the background is masked can be explained by the quality of the machine-generated masks. During verification, we noticed that the masks generated by SAM often miss legs and antennae. As a result, when masking the background, parts of the insect such as legs and antennae were also inadvertently masked, which may explain the slight drop in performance compared to the original images.


We will make the processing pipeline, the bounding boxes, and the valid masks publicly available so that other researchers can also investigate the explainability of their model when developing OSR algorithms.






# Comparison to BIOSCAN


Thank you for suggesting that we compare Open-Insect with BIOSCAN-1M (B-1M) and BIOSCAN-5M (B-5M). We discuss the similarities and differences below and will summarize them in our paper.


- Taxonomic level: All three datasets focus on insects. B-1M and B-5M mainly focus on flies and use Barcode Index Numbers (BINs) as labels (< 10% of these BINs correspond to species, while others are higher order taxonomic groups of various levels). Our dataset focuses on moths and all samples are identified to species level. This allows us to evaluate the difficulty of OSR in highly fine-grained recognition and at specified taxonomic levels.


- Data type: While all three datasets include images, the image types are different. Open-Insect contains images of museum specimens and live insects in the wild. B-1M and B-5M consist of microscope images of specimens collected using Malaise traps. While Malaise trap specimens are often too small and mangled for species-level identification, Open-Insect was designed to support species-level identification and new species discovery, focusing on more readily identifiable camera trap images, as well as slightly larger insects that can be visually identified. 
- Benchmark tasks: The intended applications of B-1M and B-5M are very different from those of Open-Insect. B-1M and B-5M assess the effectiveness of multi-modality by aligning image data and DNA barcodes. Open-Insect is designed for visual species identification where DNA barcodes may not be available.  
Given the strong covariate shift and difference in tasks between B-1M / B-5M and Open-Insect, it is not possible to directly evaluate OSR performance of models trained on B-1M and B-5M using Open-Insect. However, we include experimental results with BioCLIP, which used BIOSCAN-1M as part of the training data and was trained with images of live insects from community science platforms.




# The Choice of Pretrained Weights
Thank you very much for this question. We will clarify why we used ImageNet-1K pretrained weights instead of BioCLIP and discuss our additional experimental results with BioCLIP.


## Why ImageNet-1K?
We would first like to clarify that models for OOD detection benchmarks are usually trained from scratch, as was done in the OpenOOD benchmark. Hence, the main results we reported in Table 2 were obtained by only training models with Open-Insect. 


Since it has been shown that using ImageNet pretrained weights can help closed-set accuracy [1] and that there is a positive correlation between the closed-set and open-set performance [2], we did an ablation study to see if it holds for Open-Insect as well. We chose ImageNet-1K as there are no moth images in this dataset. Since our benchmark is designed to closely mimic real-world species discovery scenarios, OOD species should not be present in either the training or pre-training sets, as such data would not be available in practice. 


This is also the reason why we did not use weights from BioCLIP in the original paper, as some OOD species in Open-Insect overlap with those in Tree-of-Life 10M, the training set of BioCLIP. However, you are right that such experiments could be instructive, especially as BioCLIP is increasingly used for biodiversity-related tasks.


Accordingly, we conducted additional experiments to evaluate the OSR performance obtained directly from BioCLIP as well as models pretrained on BioCLIP data.


[1] Van Horn, Grant, et al. "Benchmarking Representation Learning for Natural World Image Collections." 2021 IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR). IEEE, 2021.


[2] Vaze, Sagar, et al. "Open-Set Recognition: A Good Closed-Set Classifier is All You Need." International Conference on Learning Representations.












## OSR performance of BioCLIP


Since not all ID species of Open-Insect are included in BioCLIP’s training set and some OOD species overlap with BioCLIP’s training data, we evaluated BioCLIP’s performance on a subset of Open-Insect.  We include ID species that are included in Tree-of-Life 10M or "seen" by BioCLIP and OOD species that are “unseen” to evaluate its OSR performance. summary.value: The paper introduces a large-scale insect dataset for open-set recognition. It benchmarks the performance of the other 36 open-set recognition methods and explores the benefit of auxiliary training data.

strengths_contributions.value: Open-Insect is a large-scale and extremely fine-grained dataset focusing on insects, a highly diverse and understudied taxonomic group. Unlike existing open-set recognition benchmarks that target well-studied vertebrates, this dataset offers a valuable resource for evaluating model performance on new species detection in a challenging and ecologically important domain.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
The composition and distribution of the dataset are not clearly described. The authors state that Open-Insect is based on the AMI dataset, which includes 5,364 moth species and 12 groups of non-moth arthropods, but no further details are provided. A more thorough explanation, a comparison with the original AMI dataset, and a visualization of the Open-Insect's taxonomic distribution would help clarify what is included. Being explicit about the dataset’s content is essential, and this information is currently missing.

The paper is generally well-written, but some parts are overloaded with abbreviations, which makes them difficult to follow.

In Table 2, several reported standard deviations for post-hoc methods are quite substantial. Since the results are based on only three training runs, this level of variability raises concerns about the stability and reproducibility of the reported performance. I recommend increasing the number of runs to better estimate mean performance and reduce uncertainty. At a minimum, the authors should comment on the source of this variability and discuss whether the observed differences across methods are statistically significant given the high variance.

Figure 4 and its explanation are confusing. It would benefit from clearer annotations and a more detailed explanation in the text.

summary.value: The paper proposes Open-Insect, a dataset consisting of several existing insect datasets, to simulate OOD nature of species identification task. The authors create three kinds of OOD splits for evaluation: 1) local OOD; 2) non-local OOD and 3) non-moth. These splits reflect geographic-level and species-level distribution shift in the real world. The authors benchmark 38 OOD methods on these splits and further evaluate the methods on an in-the-wild OOD dataset. The experiments reveal that simple post-hoc methods are effective on the task of OOD and training with additional auxiliary data improves OOD performance.

strengths_contributions.value:
1. The paper proposes open-insect dataset, which is a compilation of existing datasets which simulates OOD nature of real world biodiversity and species identification task in the wild.
2. Extensive benchmark of 38 OOD methods is presented on the task of detecting OOD species. These include post-hoc methods, training time regularization methods and techniques that use auxiliary data.
3. Overall a solid paper with meaningful motivation and good writing.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
1. My major concern is that some models can simply rely on background spurious features to detect if a sample is OOD rather than focusing on fine-grained species-level features. The background features of the lab or camera traps (for in the wild evaluation) that the insect specimens are sampled in can be enough to tell if some sample is OOD. Any thoughts on the explainability aspect of the trained models?
2. The paper does not discuss the similarities and overlap of the compiled dataset with other insect benchmarks such as BIOSCAN-1M and BIOSCAN-5M. How would a model trained on such a large-scale insect dataset perform on the task of OSR?
3. Some of the benchmarks use ImageNet-1k pretrained weights. Any specific reason for using ImageNet-1k weights as opposed to weights from a foundation model such as BioCLIP? I would have liked to see performance of such domain specific models on this task.

ethical_considerations.value: No, there are no or only very minor ethics concerns

ethical_comments.value: Appropriate discussion on societal impacts is included in the paper. Licenses to the datasets compiled int he paper have been mentioned in the checklist.

dataset_code_comments.value: Yes the authors have provided the dataset and code to be able to reproduce the experiments done in the paper.

additional_feedback.value: A solid paper with a simulated dataset contribution and extensive benchmarks. There is a minor gap in evaluation related to the explainability aspect of the models. Once this gap is addressed, I am willing to raise my score.

final_justification.value: The paper explores out-of-distribution (OOD) detection of novel insect species and benchmarks several OOD detection methods on their proposed dataset. I had some concerns regarding the explainability aspect of the problem, which the authors have sufficiently addressed in the rebuttal. Therefore, I have updated my score and am leaning towards acceptance.

summary.value:
A fine-grained open-set image recognition protocol for an existing dataset is proposed.
Particularly, images of insects (moths) are separated into classes for in-distribution (ID) and Out-of-Distribution (OOD) data.
Experiments are run with many different algorithms, revealing that simple post-processing methods perform well in most cases.

strengths_contributions.value:
+ The proposed protocol is divided into local-specific groups.
+ Auxiliary data is clearly defined, and separated from ID and OOD data.
+ Samples that are non-moth insects appear during testing.
+ The authors assured that the pre-training dataset (ImageNet) has no class overlap with their benchmark.
+ A large amount of experiments are performed using many state-of-the-art methods for OSR.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
1. The major limitation in this work is that evaluation makes use of inappropriate metrics (AUROC), as largely discussed in [Dhamija2018,Wang2022]. The evaluation needs to be performed with more modern (AUOSCR, OpenAUC) [Vaze2022,Wang2022] and application-oriented metrics (OSCR, OOSA) [Dhamija2018,Cruz2024].

2. Minor issues include:

  a) The terms ID and OOD might be misleading. OOD typically refers to samples that belong to different distributions, which might include various challenges, such as different imaging conditions of the ID samples or alike, see [Wang2024].

  b) In section 2.1, the authors list Outlier Exposure as the first method to make use of auxiliary data, but earlier methods exist [Dhamija2018].
  
  c) The references include a lot of arXiv publications, where in most cases peer-reviewed publications exist.



- [Dhamija2018] Dhamija, Gunther, Boult: "Reducing network agnostophobia," NeurIPS 2018.
- [Wang2022] Wang, Xu, Yang, He, Cao, Huang: "OpenAUC: Towards AUC-Oriented open-set recognition," NeuRIPS 2022.
- [Vaze2022] Vaze, Han, Vedaldi, Zissermann: "Open-set recognition: A good closed-set classifier is all you need?" ICLR 2022.
- [Cruz2024] Cruz, Rabinowitz, Gunther, Boult: "Operational open-set recognition and PostMax refinement," ECCV 2024.
- [Wang2024] Wang, Vaze, Han: "Dissecting out-of-distribution detection and open-set recognition: a critical analysis of methods and benchmarks," IJCV 2024.

ethical_considerations.value: No, there are no or only very minor ethics concerns

dataset_code_comments.value: I did not check the code or the data.

additional_feedback.value: I would strongly suggest the authors to use modern evaluation metrics in their benchmarks, so that the community finally moves away from the old, inappropriate metrics to more meaningful ones.

final_justification.value: The authors have addressed all my issues. When they include my final remarks into their camera-ready version, I am happy to raise my rating to Accept.

title.value: Open-Insect: Benchmarking Open-Set Recognition of Novel Species in Biodiversity Monitoring

value: Biodiversity; Ecology; Species Recognition; Open-set Recognition; Open-world Machine Learning; Entomology

TLDR.value: We propose a new open-set recognition dataset, Open-Insect, and evaluate 38 algorithms for new species detection on geographical open-set splits with varying difficulty.

abstract.value:
Global biodiversity is declining at an unprecedented rate, yet little information is
known about most species and how their populations are changing. Indeed, some
90% Earth’s species are estimated to be completely unknown. Machine learning has
recently emerged as a promising tool to facilitate long-term, large-scale biodiversity
monitoring, including algorithms for fine-grained classification of species from
images. However, such algorithms typically are not designed to detect examples
from categories unseen during training – the problem of open-set recognition
(OSR) – limiting their applicability for highly diverse, poorly studied taxa such as
insects. To address this gap, we introduce Open-Insect, a large-scale, fine-grained
dataset to evaluate unknown species detection across different geographic regions
with varying difficulty. We benchmark 38 OSR algorithms across three categories:
post-hoc, training-time regularization, and training with auxiliary data, finding that
simple post-hoc approaches remain a strong baseline. We also demonstrate how to
leverage auxiliary data to improve species discovery in regions with limited data.
Our results provide timely insights to guide the development of computer vision
methods for biodiversity monitoring and species discovery.
